blocks.text:
Angela Mahoney
General Manager
Johnson, Cross and Gibbs
Dear Ms. Mahoney,

This letter sets out the terms on which we will carry out a service line assessment for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}, and I am glad to be putting them in writing, because a shared understanding of the work is worth as much at the outset as any finding we will hand you at the end. What follows describes the scope we have agreed, the people who will do the work, the fee and when it begins, and the standard terms we both sign up to. If any part of it reads differently from the conversation we had, please say so before you countersign, so that the document we both hold to is the same one.
The work we have agreed

The assessment looks at your service lines and asks a plain question of each of them, which is whether it earns its keep once its true costs are set honestly against what it actually brings in. We will build that picture from your own cost accounting and volumes rather than from national benchmarks alone, because a line that looks marginal against an outside figure often looks quite different once its local economics are laid out in full. Where a line's performance turns on how physician effort is compensated, or on where the revenue cycle is losing what the line has already earned, we will follow the question into those areas rather than stop at the edge of the ledger.

Our habit is to lead with what the numbers support and to label a recommendation as a recommendation rather than dress it up as a finding, and you should expect that discipline from us throughout. Nothing we put in front of you will assert a conclusion the analysis has not earned, and where the evidence is genuinely mixed we will tell you so plainly instead of resolving it for the sake of a cleaner page. That is slower in a given week, and it is the only way we know to produce work that holds up when someone outside the room reads it closely.
Who will do the work

Daniel Alvarado, our Senior Consultant, will lead the assessment day to day and will be your point of contact for anything of substance, and he is the person who will reconcile your cost accounting until each line finally tells the truth. Susan Clark, a Principal in our advisory practice, will take up any question that touches physician compensation, and she is careful with fair-market-value language precisely because she reaches for it only where the analysis has earned it. Patricia Moore, an Analyst with us, will carry the revenue-cycle work, following a denied claim through every handoff that touched it, and she is often the one who asks the question the rest of us had assumed was already answered.

I will not run the work week to week, but I read everything before it reaches you, and I am reachable directly if the assessment is not going the way you expected. If that ever becomes your concern, I would ask you to call me rather than wait for the next scheduled update.
Fee and when we begin

Our fee for the assessment is {{fact:f:E-2020-001.fee}}, fixed at the outset so that neither of us has to reopen the commercial question once the work is under way. We expect the assessment to run roughly seven months from commencement, and the work begins on {{fact:f:E-2020-001.start}}. The terms below set out how that fee is billed and the small number of protections we each carry.
Fees and payment

The fixed fee is billed in equal monthly installments across the term of the assessment, the first on your countersignature and the commencement of the work and the remainder on the same day of each month thereafter, without regard to the particular stage the assessment has reached in any given month. Reasonable and documented out-of-pocket costs, meaning travel to your sites and any external data or verification you ask us to commission, are billed at cost as incurred and itemized on each invoice. Invoices are payable within thirty days of receipt.
Term and termination

The engagement runs from the commencement date named above until we deliver the completed assessment, and either of us may end it earlier on thirty days' written notice. If you end it, you owe the installments that have fallen due as of that date together with the costs incurred to that point, and nothing beyond them. If we end it, which we would do only if the work as defined had become one we could not complete honestly, we will return any amount paid for work not yet performed.
Confidentiality

The information you will open to us, your cost accounting, your compensation arrangements, and the operating detail beneath them, is confidential, and we will use it only for this assessment and disclose it to no one outside the team named above without your agreement. We ask the same of you for the analysis and working materials we provide, which are yours to use inside your organization for the decisions this work is meant to inform and are not for wider circulation. Because some of what we examine touches physician compensation, we will handle that material with the added care its sensitivity deserves.
Limitation of liability

We will carry out the assessment with the care and skill customary in our profession, and we will tell you what the evidence supports, but the decisions that follow from it are yours to make and we do not warrant their outcome. The analysis rests on the completeness and accuracy of the data you provide us, and while we will test what can reasonably be tested and flag what we cannot, we do not independently audit your books. Our aggregate liability under this engagement, on any theory, is limited to the fees actually paid to us for it, and neither of us is liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss, save that nothing here limits liability for our own fraud or willful misconduct.
Governing law

This letter is the whole of our agreement on this assessment and supersedes anything said or drafted before it, and it is governed by the law of the state in which our firm keeps its principal office, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules. Any dispute we cannot settle between ourselves belongs to the courts sitting in that state, and any change to these terms is effective only in writing signed by us both.
If this reflects our agreement

If this letter matches what we agreed, please countersign where indicated and return a copy to me, and Daniel Alvarado will be in touch within the week to arrange the intake session and the first data request. I would ask that you bring the people who own the service-line and revenue-cycle numbers into that first session together, because the work goes faster and lands better when everyone who holds a piece of the picture hears the same questions at the same time.
We are glad you asked us to take this on, and we will give it the care it deserves.
With kind regards,

To: Patricia Moore, Susan Clark, Richard Marsh
From: Daniel Alvarado
Re: Kickoff, service line assessment for Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

We are engaged to tell {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} which of its service lines earn their keep and which do not, and to do it with numbers that hold up. The work commences on {{fact:f:E-2020-001.start}} and runs about seven months. Earning its keep means one thing here: a line's true cost per case, loaded honestly, set against the net revenue it actually collects. This memo is so that we all start from the same picture of what we owe the client and in what order.

Our client contact is Angela Mahoney, General Manager at Johnson, Cross and Gibbs, and anything of substance routes through her. She has said she wants findings she can take to her board and her counsel without either of them flinching. That sets our standard. Nothing leaves this team that the analysis does not carry.

Here is the shape of the seven months, so we all hold the same map. The first stretch is definitions and data. The middle is the cost reconstruction and the revenue-cycle trace, run side by side rather than one behind the other. The last stretch is the compensation review and the report. We will not call a line a winner or a loser until its full costs are in, and we will keep recommendations separate from findings on every page we write.
The lines of work

items: Service-line economics. I own this. We rebuild each line's true cost per case and set it against actual net revenue, from the client's own cost accounting rather than from benchmarks, so we can see which lines are carrying the others and by how much. This is the spine of the assessment, and the other three lines of work either feed it or check it.

Physician compensation. Susan Clark owns this. Where a line's economics turn on how physician effort is paid, she looks at whether the arrangement would survive a fair-market-value review, and she uses that phrase only where the analysis earns it.

Revenue cycle. Patricia Moore owns this. She traces where lines lose revenue they have already earned, following denied claims through every handoff, so we can tell a line that is genuinely unprofitable from one that is merely leaking.

Client data and logistics. Richard Marsh owns this. He turns the client's paperwork into something we can work from, including the material that arrives as a scan rather than a file, and he keeps the intake schedule.

blocks.text: The first two weeks

First order of business is the data request. I will have it to Angela Mahoney by the end of this week, and Richard Marsh will chase what comes back. Susan and Patricia, start scoping your samples now so we are not waiting on a full pull to begin.

I would like us all in a room for half an hour early next week to agree the service-line definitions before anyone touches a number. Getting that settled up front is what keeps us from re-running the analysis later. Bring your questions to that session rather than after it.

A word on how we will keep each other current. We will hold a short internal check-in each week, and we will send the client a written status at the points we agreed. If something one of you finds changes the plan, raise it as soon as you see it, not at the next check-in. That habit is what keeps the report free of surprises for anyone, us included.
Service Line Assessment: Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

blocks.text: Meeting Minutes: Service Line Assessment for Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

Mid-engagement working session to review progress on the service-line assessment for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} with the client's general manager, held at the client's offices. The purpose was to walk the client through the interim cost picture, agree what remains to be pulled, and set the compensation work in the frame the client's counsel will expect. Minutes recorded by Susan Clark.
Attendees

items: Susan Clark, Principal (chair)
Daniel Alvarado, Senior Consultant
Patricia Moore, Analyst
Angela Mahoney, General Manager, Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

blocks.text: Discussion

The service-line cost work is far enough along to show a shape, and the shape is that a small number of lines are carrying the rest of them. Daniel Alvarado walked the group through the reconstructed cost per case for the lines we have finished, set against actual net revenue rather than charges, and two of the larger lines the client had assumed were healthy look thinner once their full costs are loaded in. We were careful to note for the record that these are interim numbers on a partial data pull, and that no line should be labelled a loser until its costs are complete.

Patricia Moore reported that part of what reads as poor line economics is in fact revenue the client has already earned and then lost in the billing process. She has traced a sample of denied claims on the surgical lines through each handoff, and the denials cluster at a small number of points that could be fixed without touching clinical operations. Angela Mahoney asked whether the leakage could account for the whole of the gap on those lines, and the honest answer given was that it accounts for part of it, and that we will size how much of it before we say anything firmer.

On physician compensation the group agreed to move carefully. Susan Clark set out that where a line's economics depend on how physician effort is paid, the question is whether the arrangement would survive a fair-market-value review, and that we will use that phrase only where the analysis actually reaches it rather than as a loose description. Angela Mahoney confirmed that the client's general counsel will want any compensation finding presented in that frame, which is the frame we had intended to use.

On logistics, the group noted that a share of the client's contracting paperwork arrives as scanned images with no text layer, which slows the pull because the underlying detail has to be re-keyed by hand rather than read straight from a file. Angela Mahoney agreed to have the client send the remaining executed statements of work and consents, and to flag which of them exist only as scans so that our team can plan the re-keying around them. The group fixed the next working session for roughly a month out, by which point the cost reconstruction should be complete and the leakage on the surgical lines sized, and both sides agreed to keep the interim numbers inside this room until then.
Action items

rows: Finish the cost reconstruction for the two remaining service lines
Size the denied-claim leakage on the surgical lines against the cost gap
Scope the physician-compensation questions that warrant a fair-market-value review
Provide the remaining contracting files, including the scanned consents

blocks.text: Status Report: Service Line Assessment for Johnson, Cross and Gibbs
Prepared by Daniel Alvarado, Senior Consultant, for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}. This report covers the period since our last update and is confidential to you and your leadership team.
Where things stand

The assessment is at its midpoint and on schedule. We have finished the cost reconstruction for the major service lines, the revenue-cycle trace is producing numbers we can use, and the physician-compensation questions are scoped and ready for the careful part. The picture is coming into focus, and it is more nuanced than a single profitable-or-not verdict.

The short of it is that a small number of lines are carrying the rest, but the reasons differ from line to line. Some of what looks weak is a genuine cost problem. Some of it is revenue you have earned and then lost downstream. Telling those two causes apart is most of the work between now and delivery.
What we finished this period

We completed the reconstructed cost per case for every major line and set it against actual net revenue rather than charges. Two lines the organization had treated as healthy look thinner once their full costs are loaded in, and at least one line that looked marginal is in fact carrying overhead that belongs elsewhere. I want to label that plainly as a preliminary read. It is a finding the completed numbers will either confirm or correct, and I will not present it as settled before then.

Patricia Moore has traced a sample of denied claims on the surgical lines through every handoff in the billing process. The denials cluster at a few points that can be fixed without touching clinical operations. That matters, because some of what reads as weak line economics is really revenue you have already earned and then lost after the fact. We can now separate those two causes with evidence rather than assertion, which is a large part of the value here.

Susan Clark has scoped the physician-compensation work and framed it the way your general counsel will expect to see it. Where a line's economics depend on how physician effort is paid, the question is whether the arrangement would survive a fair-market-value review. We will reach for that language only where the analysis earns it, and nowhere else.

We also made real headway on the data itself, which is worth reporting because it is where an assessment like this quietly succeeds or stalls. A meaningful share of your contracting paperwork reached us as scanned images rather than files, with no text a system can read, and our team has re-keyed the detail we need from those documents by hand. The result is that the smaller lines now rest on the same quality of figures as the large ones, so no line in the analysis is a guess.
What comes next

Over the next period we finish the cost reconstruction for the remaining smaller lines and reconcile the revenue-cycle results against the service-line picture. We then move from what each line costs to why it costs that, which is the part that turns a scorecard into something you can act on. Susan Clark begins the compensation review in earnest once the line economics are final, because the two questions are linked and answering them out of order would produce a conclusion neither of us should trust.

We are also planning the handoff. When the findings are firm, Susan Clark and I would rather walk your leadership through them in person than send a report cold, so that any line you want to push on is discussed with the numbers in the room. We will propose a time for that session in the next update, and we will keep it tight and specific to the decisions in front of you.
Risks and where we need you

Two things could slow us, and neither is alarming. The first is data completeness. A share of the contracting paperwork reaches us as scans rather than files, and where the underlying detail is not machine-readable we are re-keying it by hand, which takes longer. The second is time with your finance staff for the reconciliation questions, and a few standing hours with them over the coming month would remove that risk entirely.

On budget, the work remains within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2020-001.fee}}, and nothing we currently see suggests that will change. If the scanned-document re-keying grows beyond what we have absorbed so far, I will raise it with you before it touches either the timeline or the fee, not after.
We are pleased with where the assessment sits at the halfway mark. The next report will bring you the first firm findings, line by line.
Meeting Minutes: Service Line Assessment for Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

Working session to review the draft report for the service-line assessment for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} ahead of client review, held at the client's offices in the later stage of the engagement. The purpose was to confirm the findings are final, agree how the recommendations are set apart from them, and settle what remains before the report goes to the client and its counsel. Minutes recorded by Susan Clark.
In attendance

items: Susan Clark, Principal (chair)
Daniel Alvarado, Senior Consultant
Patricia Moore, Analyst
Angela Mahoney, General Manager, Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

blocks.text: Notes from the session

The service-line findings are now firm, and they hold the shape the interim numbers had suggested. Daniel Alvarado presented the completed cost per case against net revenue for every line, and the group agreed the results are ready to go into the draft report without further reconstruction. Two lines the client had treated as healthy are in fact subsidized by the others, and the draft says so plainly, with the cost detail set out behind it. The group reviewed each line in turn and found no reconstruction still open, which means the numbers in the draft are the numbers the client will see.

Patricia Moore closed out the revenue-cycle work by quantifying the leakage on the surgical lines and separating it from the genuine cost problem. The recommendations are specific and operational, and they name the handoffs where denials originate rather than the departments, which keeps the report useful to the people who will actually fix it. Angela Mahoney asked that the recommendations be labelled as recommendations and kept apart from the findings, and Susan Clark confirmed the draft is already written that way.

On physician compensation, Susan Clark reported that the review is complete and that one arrangement warrants a closer fair-market-value look, stated in exactly those terms and no stronger. The group agreed the report will present that as a flag for the client's counsel to pursue rather than as a conclusion the assessment is entitled to draw on its own. Angela Mahoney confirmed the client's general counsel will take it from there.

On the shape of the report itself, the group agreed the findings lead and the recommendations follow, each labelled as such, with the cost detail carried in an appendix so a reader can trace any line back to its numbers. Daniel Alvarado noted that a few of the smaller lines rest partly on contracting terms that reached us only as scans, and that the report will say plainly where a number depends on re-keyed detail rather than a clean data feed. The group agreed to flag that provenance in the report so the client knows exactly what each number rests on.

The group also settled how the findings will be presented. Susan Clark and Daniel Alvarado will walk the client's leadership through the draft in person once comments are back, rather than send it cold, so that any line the client disputes is argued in the room where the numbers are to hand. Angela Mahoney will assemble the client-side reviewers, including someone from the revenue-cycle side who can confirm the leakage points are real, and will return a single consolidated set of comments rather than several.
Follow-ups

rows: Circulate the full draft report for client review
Complete the fair-market-value flag write-up for the client's counsel
Return client review comments and confirm the final presentation date
